Use that for three weeks to avoid a stomach ache, then check the veterinary clinic’s lobby brochures for the local vet’s approved starter list. They have laminated sheets with exact caloric needs for three-month-old Labs right next to the checkout counter.

As for how often, it’s usually three times a day at that size. You can set alarms on your phone for morning, afternoon, and evening to keep it regular. Don’t snack in between. The puppy’s routine sets yours, so just stick to the clock. If you miss a window, skip it and wait for the next scheduled time so you don’t confuse her stomach.

Treats are tricky because you don’t want to spoil her appetite or ruin her teeth. High-value training rewards like small pieces of boiled chicken or commercial soft-training bites are fine, but keep them under five percent of her daily calories. A good rule is one small treat per successful command. Again, the vet techs can weigh out a sample portion if you’re unsure.

Also, a lot of first-time owners join a puppy socialization circle; you’ll get meet-and-greet access and the trainer will model the correct approach distance and duration. It saves you trial and error. Catch you on the flip side.
